model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a 3x3x3 3D Tic Tac Toe game. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(board: list[list[list[int]]]) -> tuple[int, int, int]: ... ``` # State Representation - `board` is a 3x3x3 list of lists of lists. - `0` represents an empty cell. - `1` represents your move. - `-1` represents the opponent's move. - Example: `[[[0, 0, 1], ...]]` indicates the first line in the first 2 dimensions has two empty cells, and the last cell occupied by you. # Action / Return Format - Return a tuple of three integers `(i, j, k)` where each is in `0-2`. - The chosen cell must be empty. - The first integer corresponds to the first dimension of the input board, the second to the second dimension, and the third to the third dimension. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
For 3D tic-tac-toe with 27 cells, exhaustive search is infeasible, so I'm planning a robust policy: check for immediate wins, block opponent threats, then use alpha-beta minimax with iterative deepening under a time budget. I'll first enumerate all 49 winning lines across rows, face diagonals, and space diagonals before implementing the win-check logic.

The opening move should always be the center, since it's part of the most winning lines and known to be a strong first-player advantage in this variant. For deeper search efficiency I'm weighing branching factor against Python's speed, estimating that with good move ordering and alpha-beta pruning I can reach depth 5-6 within the time limit, using a leaf evaluation that scores line potential for each side.

I need to guard against running out of time mid-search by checking elapsed time periodically and falling back to the best move found at the last fully completed depth. For terminal detection I only need to check the lines passing through the most recently placed piece, which keeps win-checking cheap.

I'm generating all 49 winning lines in the 3x3x3 grid by iterating over direction vectors and canonicalizing to avoid duplicates, then mapping each cell to the lines it belongs to for fast lookups... Writing line generation code...

For the heuristic scoring, I'm counting lines where I have two pieces and an open third cell as immediate threats, weighting these highly since they represent near-wins that the opponent must block.

Now I'm sketching the negamax search with alpha-beta pruning, ordering moves by their static line-count value (center cells score highest since they intersect the most winning lines) and using the transposition table's stored best move first when available. For the transposition table key I'll just hash the full board tuple since 27 cells is small enough. I also want to add a time-check inside the node loop that raises an exception once the budget is exceeded, and to fully solve endgame positions once few empty cells remain since that's tractable to brute-force.

I'm generating all 49 winning lines by scanning every cell and all 13 direction vectors, keeping only in-bounds triples, then deduplicating. A win at a given cell for a player just means checking if any line through that cell is fully occupied by them, and the evaluation function needs to return the score from the perspective of whichever player is about to move at that node.

Now I'm working out the heuristic scoring: for each line, count how many cells belong to me versus the opponent, and if the line isn't contaminated by both sides, add or subtract a weighted value (0/1/8 for 0/1/2 matching cells) depending on whose favor it leans toward.

I'm also adding a shortcut so that if the side to move already has two-in-a-row with an open third cell, I treat that as a near-certain win (and similarly flag when the opponent has multiple such threats as a near-certain loss), since this cheap one-ply check meaningfully sharpens the evaluation before falling back to full negamax search with terminal win checks on each candidate move.

Writing the policy function...

With multiple blocks it's likely already lost, so I'll just run the search over the candidate set rather than special-casing further. I'm setting up a time-limited search with a deadline around 0.7 seconds, checking elapsed time periodically, ordering root moves by previous iteration scores, and using a transposition table keyed on board state and player to store depth, score, flag, and best move.

Writing negamax function...

Still writing negamax logic...

I'm also considering forced-move pruning: when the opponent has an immediate winning threat, I only need to search blocking moves rather than all empty cells, which drastically cuts branching—if there are two or more threats it's a forced loss, if just one, that block becomes the only move to search.

To find these threats efficiently, instead of checking each empty cell individually against every line (which is somewhat costly), I'm computing line sums in a single pass: for each of the 49 lines, summing the three cell values lets me detect two-in-a-row-plus-empty patterns for both the current player and opponent in one sweep.

Precomputing table lookup...

If opp has a threat, I need to find the empty cell to block it, but I have to watch for cases where two threat lines share the same empty cell versus needing to block distinct cells — that determines a forced loss. At the leaf, I'll weight two-in-a-rows more heavily than single lines in the scoring heuristic, since immediate wins are already handled separately.

Estimating speed: with tuple lookups this is roughly 20k nodes/sec in Python, giving maybe 10k nodes in a 0.7s budget, enough for depth 4-5 with alpha-beta and forced-block pruning — solid against weaker opponents. A full precomputed solution isn't feasible since the state space is far too large to fit in 1 second without shipping a lookup table, so I'll stick with search plus heuristics rather than perfect play.

I'll optimize the inner loop by keeping line data as tuples and using local variable caching, and rely on detecting mixed +1/-1 lines for win/threat checks. When the opponent has exactly one threat, I only need to search the forced blocking move since anything else loses immediately, and this also means forks (two threats after our move) get caught automatically at shallow depth since the opponent's resulting node sees an unstoppable double threat. For move ordering I'll try the transposition table move first, then fall back to heuristics favoring central and corner cells.

At the root I'll do iterative deepening, keeping the best move from each completed depth and reusing that ordering, with a time budget around 0.55 seconds to stay safely under a one-second limit accounting for Python overhead. If the opponent has multiple threats and we can't win outright, I'll just search among the blocking candidates without special-casing further.

Writing search code...

Writing negamax with transposition table...

Still writing scoring logic...

For each line I check who's winning it, adding weighted bonuses for near-wins and tracking which empty cell would block an opponent's threat. I'm noting that win detection happens earlier, so mine==3 or theirs==3 shouldn't actually occur here.

I still need to compute how many empty cells remain — tracking this via root empties minus ply avoids rescanning the board each time. If there are two or more blocking threats simultaneously, that's a forced loss next move, otherwise I collect the single blocking move as a forced reply.

For depth exhaustion, I'll fall back to the static score, but single forced-block sequences should still recurse regardless of depth since they only branch one way and are cheap to extend. Moves get ordered by heuristic priority with the transposition table move promoted to the front, and at the root I iterate through increasing search depths starting from the best-ordered candidate.

On timeout I keep the results from the last fully completed iteration rather than trusting partial scores mid-iteration, unless a partial result already reveals a forced win, in which case I take it immediately.

For root move ordering, I score each candidate with negamax using the standard alpha update rather than a strict fail-soft window, which is close enough for ordering purposes even if some bounds are inexact.

I'll cap the search depth to iterate up through the number of empty cells, and wrap the whole thing in error handling that falls back to picking the first available empty cell if anything goes wrong.
